stem:
An oxide of iron contains 69.9% iron, its empirical formula is:
(Given : Molar mass of Fe and O are 56 and 16 g mol$^{-1}$ respectively.)

formulas: Simplest whole-number mole ratio gives the empirical formula

steps.text: In 100 g of the oxide: $m_{\ce{Fe}} = 69.9$ g and $m_{\ce{O}} = 100 - 69.9 = 30.1$ g.
Simplest ratio $\ce{Fe} : \ce{O} = 1.248 : 1.881 = 1 : 1.507 \approx 2 : 3$, so the empirical formula is $\ce{Fe2O3}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting to get the oxygen mass by subtracting from 100 g
Rounding 1.507 to 1 instead of recognising $1.5 = 3/2$
solution.final_check: $\ce{Fe2O3}$ contains $112/160 = 70.0\%$ Fe, matching the given 69.9%.

stem: If shortest wavelength of hydrogen atom in Lyman series is $x$, then longest wavelength in Balmer series of $\ce{He+}$ is:

steps.text: Shortest Lyman wavelength for H ($Z = 1$): $n_2 = \infty \to n_1 = 1$ gives $\frac{1}{x} = R(1-0) = R$, so $x = 1/R$.
Longest Balmer wavelength for $\ce{He+}$ ($Z = 2$): $n_2 = 3 \to n_1 = 2$ gives $\frac{1}{\lambda} = 4R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right) = 4R\cdot\frac{5}{36} = \frac{5R}{9}$.
Hence $\lambda = \frac{9}{5R} = \frac{9x}{5}$.

pitfalls: Using the H-atom ($Z=1$) formula for $\ce{He+}$ — the $Z^2 = 4$ factor is essential
Mixing up longest/shortest with the $n = 3 	o 2$ vs $n = \infty 	o 2$ transitions
solution.final_check: Longest wavelength needs the smallest gap ($3 \to 2$); the $Z^2$ factor correctly shortens it versus H.

Match the LIST-I with LIST-II
List-I (Orbital) | List-II (Radial nodes and nodal plane)
A. 2s | I. 1 Radial node + two nodal planes
B. 3s | II. 1 Radial node + one nodal plane
C. 3p | III. 2 Radial nodes + No nodal plane
D. 4d | IV. 1 Radial node + No nodal plane
Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below:

steps.text: 2s ($n=2, l=0$): $2-0-1 = 1$ radial node, $0$ nodal planes $\to$ IV.
3s ($n=3, l=0$): $3-0-1 = 2$ radial nodes, $0$ nodal planes $\to$ III.
3p ($n=3, l=1$): $3-1-1 = 1$ radial node, $1$ nodal plane $\to$ II.
4d ($n=4, l=2$): $4-2-1 = 1$ radial node, $2$ nodal planes $\to$ I. Hence A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

pitfalls: Confusing radial nodes ($n-l-1$) with total nodes ($n-1$)
Calling every angular node a 'nodal plane' is fine for p/d, but s has none
solution.final_check: 2s indeed has one spherical radial node and no angular node — consistent with IV.

stem: The pairs among A = [$\ce{SO3^2-}$, $\ce{CO3^2-}$], B = [$\ce{O2^2-}$, $\ce{F2}$], C = [$\ce{CN-}$, $\ce{CO}$], D = [$\ce{NH3}$, $\ce{H3O+}$] and E = [$\ce{MnO4^2-}$, $\ce{CrO4^2-}$] that do not have similar Lewis dot structure are

formulas: Similar Lewis structure $\Leftrightarrow$ same skeletal connectivity, bond order and lone-pair count on the central atom

steps.text: Pair A: $\ce{SO3^2-}$ has S with 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair (pyramidal), while $\ce{CO3^2-}$ has C with 3 bond pairs and no lone pair (planar) $\to$ not similar.
Pairs B, C, D are similar: $\ce{O2^2-}$/$\ce{F2}$ (single bond, 3 lone pairs per atom), $\ce{CN-}$/$\ce{CO}$ (isoelectronic, triple bond), $\ce{NH3}$/$\ce{H3O+}$ (3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair each).
Pair E: $\ce{MnO4^2-}$ has Mn(VI), $d^1$ (an unpaired electron), whereas $\ce{CrO4^2-}$ has Cr(VI), $d^0$ $\to$ not similar.
So the pairs lacking similar Lewis dot structures are A and E.

pitfalls: Treating $\ce{MnO4^2-}$ and $\ce{CrO4^2-}$ as identical just because both are tetrahedral oxoanions — the $d^1$ vs $d^0$ difference matters
Missing the lone pair on S in $\ce{SO3^2-}$
solution.final_check: Only option B lists exactly the two dissimilar pairs, A and E.

stem:
Arrange the following isothermal processes in order of the magnitude of the work (p – V) involved between states 1 and 2.
A. Expansion in single stage $w_A$
B. Expansion in multi stages $w_B$
C. Compression in single stage $w_C$
D. Compression in multi stages $w_D$
Choose the correct option.

steps.text: Expansion: splitting into more stages keeps $p_{ext}$ higher at each step, so more work is done by the gas: $|w_B| > |w_A|$ (reversible expansion is the maximum).
Compression: single-stage compression holds $p_{ext}$ at the full initial pressure throughout, needing the most work input: $|w_C| > |w_D|$ (reversible compression is the minimum).
Between the same states, every compression magnitude exceeds every expansion magnitude (since $p_{ext} \ge p_{gas}$ in compression): $|w_C| > |w_D| > |w_B| > |w_A|$.

pitfalls: Comparing signed work instead of magnitudes — expansion work is negative by convention
Thinking multi-stage compression needs more work (it needs less)
solution.final_check: On a p–V plot the single-stage compression rectangle encloses the largest area — consistent with $w_C$ largest.

stem: When 0.25 moles of a non-volatile, non-ionizable solute was dissolved in 1 mole of a solvent the vapor pressure of solution was $x$ % of vapor pressure of pure solvent. What is $x$ %?

steps.text: Raoult's law for a non-volatile solute: $p = p^\circ X_{\text{solvent}}$.
Hence $p = 0.80\,p^\circ$, i.e. $x = 80$.

pitfalls: Using the solute mole fraction (0.20) as the answer instead of the solvent's
Forgetting that a non-ionizable solute has van't Hoff factor $i = 1$
solution.final_check: Mole fraction of solvent $0.8$ directly gives 80% of the pure vapour pressure.

stem:
One mole each of He and A(g) are taken in a 10 L closed flask and heated to 400 K to establish the following equilibrium.
$\ce{A(g) <=> B(g)}$
$K_c$ for this reaction at 400 K is 4.0. The partial pressures (in atm) of He and B(g) are respectively (at equilibrium)
(Assume He, A(g) and B(g) behave as ideal gases)
(Given : R = 0.082 L atm K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$)

steps.text: Let $x$ mol of A convert to B: $K_c = \dfrac{x}{1-x} = 4.0 \Rightarrow x = 4(1-x) \Rightarrow x = 0.80$ mol of B at equilibrium.
He is inert, so $n_{\ce{He}} = 1$ mol throughout.
$p_{\ce{He}} = \dfrac{1 \times 0.082 \times 400}{10} = 3.28$ atm and $p_B = \dfrac{0.80 \times 0.082 \times 400}{10} = 2.624$ atm.

pitfalls: Letting He participate in the equilibrium — it is inert
Swapping the order: the question asks for He first, then B
solution.final_check: $p_B/p_A = 0.8/0.2 = 4 = K_c$ (with $\Delta n_g = 0$, $K_p = K_c$); He pressure is untouched by the reaction.

Consider the following data.
Electrolyte | $\Lambda^\circ_m$ (S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$)
$\ce{BaCl2}$ | $x_1$
$\ce{H2SO4}$ | $x_2$
$\ce{HCl}$ | $x_3$
$\ce{BaSO4}$ is sparingly soluble in water. If the conductivity of the saturated $\ce{BaSO4}$ solution is $x$ S cm$^{-1}$ then the solubility product of $\ce{BaSO4}$ can be given as
(Here $\Lambda_m = \Lambda^\circ_m$)

steps.text: Kohlrausch's law: $\Lambda^\circ_m(\ce{BaSO4}) = x_1 + x_2 - 2x_3$.
Solubility $s = \dfrac{1000\kappa}{\Lambda_m} = \dfrac{1000x}{\alpha(x_1+x_2-2x_3)}$ mol L$^{-1}$; with $\Lambda_m = \Lambda^\circ_m$ the degree of dissociation $\alpha = 1$.

pitfalls: Dropping the factor 1000 when converting $\kappa$ (S cm$^{-1}$) with $\Lambda_m$ (S cm$^2$ mol$^{-1}$) to mol L$^{-1}$
Wrong Kohlrausch combination — the HCl term is subtracted twice
solution.final_check: Units check: $(1000 \times \mathrm{S\,cm^{-1}} / \mathrm{S\,cm^2\,mol^{-1}})^2 = \mathrm{mol^2\,L^{-2}}$, correct for $K_{sp}$.

stem:
Given below are two statements:
**Statement I:** Aluminium is more electropositive than thallium as the standard electrode potential value of E°$_{\ce{Al^3+}/\ce{Al}}$ is negative and E°$_{\ce{Tl^3+}/\ce{Tl}}$ is positive.
**Statement II:** The sum of first three ionization enthalpies of boron is very high when compared to that of aluminium. Due to this reason boron forms covalent compounds only and aluminium forms $\ce{Al^3+}$ ion.
In the light of the above statements, choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
options.B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
options.C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
options.D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true

formulas: More negative $E^\circ_{M^{3+}/M} \Rightarrow$ metal more easily oxidised $\Rightarrow$ more electropositive

steps.text: Statement I: $E^\circ_{\ce{Al^3+}/\ce{Al}} = -1.66$ V (negative) while $E^\circ_{\ce{Tl^3+}/\ce{Tl}}$ is positive ($\approx +0.72$ V); the more negative reduction potential means Al is oxidised more readily, i.e. Al is more electropositive $\to$ true.

Statement II: $IE_1 + IE_2 + IE_3$ for B ($801+2427+3660 = 6888$ kJ mol$^{-1}$) far exceeds Al's ($577+1817+2745 = 5139$ kJ mol$^{-1}$); the prohibitive energy cost stops $\ce{B^3+}$ from forming so boron stays covalent, while Al readily forms $\ce{Al^3+} \to$ true.

pitfalls: Reading 'more negative $E^\circ$' as 'less electropositive' — it is the reverse
Ignoring the inert-pair effect context: Tl indeed favours +1, consistent with being less electropositive
solution.final_check: Both statements are standard group-13 facts with no reversal — both true.

stem:
The **correct** statements among the following are.
A. Basic vanadium oxide is used in the manufacture of $\ce{H2SO4}$.
B. The spin-only magnetic moment value of the transition metal halide employed in Ziegler-Natta polymerization is 2.84 BM.
C. The p-block metal compound employed in Ziegler-Natta polymerization has the metal in +3 oxidation state.
D. The number of electrons present in the outer most 'd' orbital of metal halide employed in Wacker process is 8.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

steps.text: A: the contact-process catalyst is $\ce{V2O5}$, an acidic (not basic) oxide $\to$ false.
B: the Ziegler–Natta halide is $\ce{TiCl4}$ ($\ce{Ti^{4+}}$, $d^0$, $\mu = 0$) or $\ce{TiCl3}$ ($\ce{Ti^{3+}}$, $d^1$, $\mu = 1.73$ BM); 2.84 BM would need 2 unpaired electrons $\to$ false.
C: the co-catalyst $(\ce{C2H5})_3\ce{Al}$ has Al in the +3 oxidation state $\to$ true.
D: the Wacker catalyst $\ce{PdCl2}$ has $\ce{Pd^{2+}}$, a $d^8$ ion, so 8 electrons occupy the outermost d orbitals $\to$ true.

pitfalls: Calling $\ce{V2O5}$ a basic oxide — it is acidic
Assigning 2.84 BM to the Ti halide without checking the d-electron count
solution.final_check: Exactly C and D are true, matching option C.

Match the LIST-I with LIST-II
List-I (Electronic configuration of tetrahedral metal ion) | List-II (Crystal Field Stabilization Energy ($\Delta_t$))
A. $d^2$ | I. $-0.6$
B. $d^4$ | II. $-0.8$
C. $d^6$ | III. $-1.2$
D. $d^8$ | IV. $-0.4$
Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below:

formulas: Tetrahedral: $e$ set at $-0.6\Delta_t$, $t_2$ set at $+0.4\Delta_t$; always high-spin

steps.text: Tetrahedral splitting is inverted relative to octahedral: $e$ ($d_{z^2}, d_{x^2-y^2}$) lower, $t_2$ higher; all tetrahedral complexes are high-spin.
Hence A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

pitfalls: Using the octahedral ordering ($t_{2g}$ lower) for a tetrahedral complex
Pairing electrons in tetrahedral complexes — they are always high-spin
solution.final_check: The CFSE values $-1.2, -0.4, -0.6, -0.8$ vary symmetrically about $d^5$, as expected for high-spin filling.

stem:
Which of the following are true about the energy of the given d-orbitals of a tetrahedral complex?
A. $d_{xy} = d_{xz} > d_{x^2-y^2}$
B. $d_{xy} = d_{yz} > d_{z^2}$
C. $d_{x^2-y^2} > d_{z^2} > d_{xz}$
D. $d_{x^2-y^2} = d_{z^2} < d_{xz}$
Choose the correct answer from the given below:

formulas: Tetrahedral: $e$ ($d_{z^2}, d_{x^2-y^2}$) lower $<$ $t_2$ ($d_{xy}, d_{xz}, d_{yz}$) higher

steps.text: In tetrahedral geometry the $t_2$ set ($d_{xy}, d_{xz}, d_{yz}$) is higher in energy and the $e$ set ($d_{z^2}, d_{x^2-y^2}$) is lower.
A: $d_{xy}, d_{xz} \in t_2$ (degenerate) $> d_{x^2-y^2} \in e \to$ true. B: $d_{xy}, d_{yz} \in t_2$ (degenerate) $> d_{z^2} \in e \to$ true.
C: claims $d_{x^2-y^2} > d_{z^2}$, but both belong to the degenerate $e$ set $\to$ false. D: $d_{x^2-y^2} = d_{z^2}$ (both $e$) $< d_{xz}$ ($t_2$) $\to$ true.
True statements: A, B, D.

pitfalls: Splitting d-orbitals as in an octahedral field ($t_{2g} < e_g$)
solution.final_check: Every true statement respects the single rule $e < t_2$ for tetrahedral fields.

stem: $R_f$ value for 2-methylpropene in a solvent system (Ethyl acetate + ether) is 0.42. 2-methylpropene is treated with dilute $\ce{H2SO4}$ to give major organic product (X). $R_f$ value for (X) in the same solvent system under identical condition will be:

formulas: More polar compound $\to$ stronger adsorption on silica $\to$ smaller $R_f$

steps.text: Dilute $\ce{H2SO4}$ hydrates 2-methylpropene by Markovnikov addition: $(\ce{CH3})_2\ce{C=CH2} + \ce{H2O} \to (\ce{CH3})_3\ce{COH}$ (tert-butanol), the major product X.
An alcohol is much more polar than the starting alkene, so it adsorbs more strongly on the silica stationary phase and travels a shorter distance: $R_f(X) < R_f(\text{alkene}) = 0.42$.
Among the options, only 0.12 lies below 0.42.

pitfalls: Choosing a larger $R_f$ — higher polarity lowers $R_f$, not raises it
Misidentifying X (e.g. as the anti-Markovnikov alcohol)
solution.final_check: A polar product must have a smaller $R_f$; 0.12 is the only option below 0.42.

**Statement I:** 2,6-diethylcyclohexanone and 6-methyl-2-n-propylcyclohexanone are metamers.
**Statement II:** 2,2,6,6-tetramethylcyclohexanone exhibits keto-enol tautomerism.
In the light of the above statements, choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
options.B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
options.C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
options.D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true

formulas: Metamers: same molecular formula, same functional group, different alkyl groups about the functional group
Keto–enol tautomerism requires at least one $\alpha$-hydrogen

steps.text: Statement I: both compounds are $\ce{C10H18O}$ ketones differing only in the distribution of alkyl groups around the $\ce{C=O}$ (2,6-diethyl vs 2-propyl-6-methyl) — exactly the definition of metamers $\to$ true.
Statement II: in 2,2,6,6-tetramethylcyclohexanone both $\alpha$-carbons (C-2 and C-6) are quaternary and bear no hydrogen, so no enol can form $\to$ false.

pitfalls: Confusing metamers with position isomers
Assuming every ketone shows keto–enol tautomerism regardless of $\alpha$-H
solution.final_check: No $\alpha$-hydrogen means no enol form is possible — II is unambiguously false while I fits metamerism.

**Statement I:** Methane can be prepared by decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate, Kolbe's electrolysis of sodium acetate and reaction of $\ce{CH3MgBr}$ with water.
**Statement II:** Methane cannot be prepared from unsaturated hydrocarbons and by Wurtz reaction.
In the light of the above statements, choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
options.B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
options.C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
options.D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true

steps.text: Statement I: soda-lime decarboxylation of sodium ethanoate gives $\ce{CH4}$ and $\ce{CH3MgBr} + \ce{H2O} \to \ce{CH4}$ also works — but Kolbe's electrolysis of acetate liberates ethane ($\ce{C2H6}$) at the anode, not methane. Since one listed route fails, the whole statement is false.

Statement II: hydrogenation of unsaturated hydrocarbons retains the carbon skeleton (no $\ce{CH4}$), and Wurtz coupling of $\ce{CH3X}$ gives ethane — methane is inaccessible by either route $\to$ true.

pitfalls: Assuming Kolbe's electrolysis of acetate gives methane — it gives ethane
Thinking Wurtz reaction of methyl halide gives methane
solution.final_check: Exactly one route in Statement I fails (Kolbe gives ethane), while both exclusions in Statement II hold.

stem:
**Statement I:** 3-phenylpropene reacts with HBr and gives secondary alkyl bromide having a chiral carbon atom as the major product.
**Statement II:** Aryl chlorides and aryl cyanides can be prepared by Sandmeyer reaction as well as Gattermann reaction.
In the light of the above statements, choose the **correct** answer from the options given below

options.A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
options.B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
options.C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false
options.D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true

formulas: Sandmeyer: $\ce{ArN2+ ->[CuCl][HCl] ArCl}$, $\ce{ArN2+ ->[CuCN][KCN] ArCN}$; Gattermann: $\ce{ArN2+ ->[Cu][HX] ArX}$ (X = Cl, Br only)

steps.text: Statement I: $\ce{PhCH2CH=CH2} + \ce{HBr}$ adds Markovnikov to give $\ce{PhCH2CHBrCH3}$ (even allowing hydride shift to the benzylic isomer $\ce{PhCHBrCH2CH3}$, the product remains a secondary bromide whose C–Br carbon carries four different groups) $\to$ true.

Statement II: Sandmeyer gives both $\ce{ArCl}$ and $\ce{ArCN}$, but Gattermann ($\ce{Cu}$/HX) furnishes only $\ce{ArCl}$/$\ce{ArBr}$ — aryl cyanides are not obtained by Gattermann. The 'as well as' claim is therefore false.

pitfalls: Forgetting that Gattermann's scope excludes cyanides
Overlooking a possible hydride shift — here it does not change the verdict
solution.final_check: Statement I holds with or without rearrangement; Statement II fails on cyanides via Gattermann.

Consider the following sequence of reactions
$\ce{(CH3)3C-OH} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) H}^+,\, \ce{PhCOOH}]{\text{(i) Cu / 573 K}} P.$
The major product P is:
(structures: A = 3-tert-butylbenzoic acid, benzene ring bearing –COOH and –C(CH$_3$)$_3$ meta to each other; B = 4-tert-butylbenzoic acid, –COOH and –C(CH$_3$)$_3$ para to each other; C = tert-butyl benzoate, $\ce{Ph-C(=O)-O-C(CH3)3}$; D = 2-methylallyl benzoate, $\ce{Ph-C(=O)-O-CH2-C(CH3)=CH2}$)

options.A: 3-tert-butylbenzoic acid: benzene ring with $\ce{-COOH}$ and $\ce{-C(CH3)3}$ in meta positions
options.B: 4-tert-butylbenzoic acid: benzene ring with $\ce{-COOH}$ and $\ce{-C(CH3)3}$ in para positions

steps.text: Step (i): a tertiary alcohol over heated Cu dehydrates to the alkene — tert-butanol gives isobutylene, $(\ce{CH3})_2\ce{C=CH2}$.

Step (ii): under acidic conditions benzoic acid adds across the $\ce{C=C}$ bond in Markovnikov fashion, placing –OCOPh on the more substituted carbon: $(\ce{CH3})_2\ce{C=CH2} + \ce{PhCOOH} \to (\ce{CH3})_3\ce{C-O-C(=O)-Ph}$.
The product is tert-butyl benzoate — option C.

pitfalls: Treating step (ii) as Fischer esterification of an alcohol — the alcohol was already consumed in step (i)
Placing the benzoate group on the terminal carbon (anti-Markovnikov)
solution.final_check: Only option C is the ester formed between benzoic acid and a tert-butyl group.
solution.dispute_note: Our answer is (C): the product formed under these conditions is tert-butyl benzoate; the key's option (B) (p-tert-butylbenzoic acid) cannot form here. Two independent blind solutions agree on (C).

verification.note: DISPUTE: Two independent blind solves give tert-butyl benzoate (C); key says p-tert-butylbenzoic acid (B) which cannot form under these conditions. Published with solver answer.

Arrange the following compounds according to increasing order of boiling points.
n-$\ce{C4H9OH}$ (A), n-$\ce{C4H9NH2}$ (B), n-$\ce{C4H10}$ (C) and $\ce{C2H5NHC2H5}$ (D).

formulas: Boiling point: van der Waals $<$ H-bonding (amine) $<$ H-bonding (alcohol); $1^\circ$ amine $>$ $2^\circ$ amine

steps.text: n-butane (C) has only weak van der Waals forces $\to$ lowest boiling point.
Both amines H-bond, but the $2^\circ$ amine D (diethylamine) H-bonds less extensively than the $1^\circ$ amine B (n-butylamine) $\to$ C < D < B.
Alcohols H-bond more strongly (O–H···O) than amines, so n-butanol (A) boils highest: C < D < B < A.

pitfalls: Ranking the $2^\circ$ amine above the $1^\circ$ amine
Placing the alkane above any H-bonded compound
solution.final_check: Actual bps — butane $\approx 0^\circ$C < diethylamine $\approx 56^\circ$C < n-butylamine $\approx 78^\circ$C < n-butanol $\approx 118^\circ$C — follow the same order.

stem:
Match the LIST-I with LIST-II
List-I (Deficiency Disease) | List-II (Vitamin)
A. Scurvy | I. Pyridoxine
B. Convulsions | II. Vitamin A
C. Cheilosis | III. Ascorbic Acid
D. Xerophthalmia | IV. Riboflavin
Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below:

formulas: Scurvy $\leftrightarrow$ vitamin C; convulsions $\leftrightarrow$ vitamin B$_6$; cheilosis $\leftrightarrow$ vitamin B$_2$; xerophthalmia $\leftrightarrow$ vitamin A

steps.text: Scurvy is the classic vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency $\to$ III. Convulsions arise from pyridoxine (B$_6$) deficiency $\to$ I.
Cheilosis (cracking at the corners of the mouth) signals riboflavin (B$_2$) deficiency $\to$ IV. Xerophthalmia (dryness of the eye) signals vitamin A deficiency $\to$ II.
Hence A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

pitfalls: Swapping pyridoxine and riboflavin (both are B-complex vitamins)
Linking xerophthalmia to vitamin D instead of A
solution.final_check: Each disease maps to its textbook vitamin: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

stem:
Match the LIST-I with LIST-II
List-I (Amino acid) | List-II (Positive reaction/Test for functional group present in side chain of amino acid)
A. Glutamine | I. Hinsberg's test
B. Lysine | II. Neutral $\ce{FeCl3}$ test
C. Tyrosine | III. Ceric ammonium nitrate test
D. Serine | IV. Hoffman bromamide degradation
Choose the **correct** answer from the options given below:

formulas: Amide $\to$ Hoffmann bromamide degradation; $1^\circ$ amine $\to$ Hinsberg test; phenol $\to$ neutral $\ce{FeCl3}$; alcohol $\to$ ceric ammonium nitrate test

steps.text: Glutamine's side chain is an amide (–$\ce{CH2CH2CONH2}$) $\to$ Hoffmann bromamide degradation $\to$ IV. Lysine's side chain is a primary amine (–$(\ce{CH2})_4\ce{NH2}$) $\to$ Hinsberg's test $\to$ I.
Tyrosine's side chain is a phenol $\to$ neutral $\ce{FeCl3}$ (violet colour) $\to$ II. Serine's side chain is an alcohol (–$\ce{CH2OH}$) $\to$ ceric ammonium nitrate test $\to$ III.
Hence A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

pitfalls: Applying the test to the $\alpha$-amino/carboxyl groups instead of the side chain
Confusing the phenol test (FeCl$_3$) with the alcohol test (ceric ammonium nitrate)
solution.final_check: Each test targets exactly the side-chain functional group: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III.

stem:
First and second ionization enthalpies of lithium are 520 kJ mol$^{-1}$ and 7297 kJ mol$^{-1}$ respectively. Energy required to convert 3.5 mg lithium (g) into $\ce{Li^2+}$(g) [$\ce{Li(g) -> Li^2+(g)}$] is ______ kJ mol$^{-1}$. (nearest integer)
[Molar mass of Li = 7 g mol$^{-1}$]

steps.text: Forming $\ce{Li^2+}$ from $\ce{Li(g)}$ costs $IE_1 + IE_2 = 520 + 7297 = 7817$ kJ mol$^{-1}$.
Moles of Li $= \dfrac{3.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{g}}{7\ \text{g mol}^{-1}} = 5.0 \times 10^{-4}$ mol.
Energy $= 7817 \times 5.0 \times 10^{-4} = 3.9085$ kJ $\approx 4$ (nearest integer).

pitfalls: Using only $IE_1$ or only $IE_2$ instead of their sum
Forgetting to convert mg to g

Consider the following sequence of reactions.
$\ce{Ph-N=N-NH-Ph} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) Aniline (in excess)}]{\text{(i) HCl}} \xrightarrow[\text{(iv) Cool, acetic acid}]{\text{(iii) Warm 40--45}^\circ\text{C}} \text{Yellow Product (X)}$
The percentage of nitrogen in the yellow product (X) formed is ______ %.
(Nearest Integer)
(Given Molar mass in g mol$^{-1}$ H:1, C:12, N:14)

steps.text: 1,3-diphenyltriazene (diazoaminobenzene) with HCl and excess aniline, warmed to 40–45°C, rearranges to $p$-aminoazobenzene, $p$-$\ce{H2N-C6H4-N=N-Ph}$ — the yellow product X.

pitfalls: Counting only the two azo nitrogens and missing the amino nitrogen (3 N atoms in all)
Using the triazene's mass incorrectly — note it is isomeric, so the %N is unchanged either way

Sucrose hydrolyses in acidic medium into glucose and fructose by first order rate law with $t_{1/2} = 3$ hour. The percentage of sucrose remaining after 6 hours is ______.
(Nearest Integer)
(Given : log 2 = 0.3010 and log 3 = 0.4771)

steps.text: For a first-order reaction the fraction remaining after $n$ half-lives is $(1/2)^n$.
Number of half-lives in 6 hours: $n = 6/3 = 2$.
Fraction remaining $= (1/2)^2 = 1/4$, i.e. 25%.

pitfalls: Computing the percentage decomposed (75%) instead of the percentage remaining
Using the integrated rate law unnecessarily — half-life counting suffices
solution.final_check: Two half-lives leave exactly one-quarter: 25%.

Consider the reaction X $\rightleftharpoons$ Y at 300 K. If $\Delta H^\circ$ and K are 28.40 kJ mol$^{-1}$ and $1.8 \times 10^{-7}$ at the same temperature, then the magnitude of $\Delta S^\circ$ for the reaction in J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$ is ______.
(Nearest integer)
(Given : R = 8.3 J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$, ln 10 = 2.3, log 3 = 0.48, log 2 = 0.30)

steps.text: $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -8.3 \times 300 \times 2.3 \times (-6.74) = 38600$ J mol$^{-1}$.
$\Delta S^\circ = \dfrac{\Delta H^\circ - \Delta G^\circ}{T} = \dfrac{28400 - 38600}{300} = -34$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$.
Magnitude $= 34$.

pitfalls: Sign error in $\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K$ when $K < 1$ ($\ln K$ negative $\Rightarrow$ $\Delta G^\circ$ positive)
Forgetting to convert $\Delta H^\circ$ from kJ to J
solution.final_check: $\Delta G^\circ = +38.6$ kJ exceeds $\Delta H^\circ = 28.4$ kJ, so $\Delta S^\circ$ is negative with $|\Delta S^\circ| = 10.2/300$ kJ $= 34$ J K$^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $[\cdot]$ denote the greatest integer function. If the domain of the function $f(x)=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x+[x]}{3}\right)$ is $[\alpha, \beta)$, then $\alpha^2+\beta^2$ is equal to:

steps.text: $|\frac{x+[x]}{3}|\le 1$ gives $|x+[x]|\le 3$. Let $g(x)=x+[x]$, which is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$ (sum of two increasing functions).

For $x\in[-1,0)$: $g(x)=x-1\in[-2,-1)$, so $|g(x)|\le 2<3$ — the whole interval is in the domain. Just below $-1$: for $x\in[-2,-1)$, $g(x)=x-2\in[-4,-3)$; $|g(x)|\le 3$ needs $x-2\ge -3$, i.e. $x\ge -1$, impossible there. At $x=-2$, $g=-4$. Hence nothing below $-1$ qualifies, so $\alpha=-1$.
For $x\in[1,2)$: $g(x)=x+1\in[2,3)$, so $|g(x)|<3$ — included. At $x=2$: $g(2)=4>3$, excluded; for $x>2$, $g$ only grows. Hence the domain ends at $2$, with $2$ excluded: $\beta=2$.

pitfalls: Treating $[x]$ as continuous and solving $x+[x]=\pm 3$ algebraically gives spurious $x=-1.5$; the jump discontinuities of $[x]$ must be respected — check each piece $[n,n+1)$ separately.
solution.final_check: $g(-1)=-2$ (in range), $g(1.99)=2.99$ (in range), $g(2)=4$ (out): boundary behaviour confirms $[-1,2)$.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let one root of the quadratic equation in $x$: $(k^2-15k+27)x^2+9(k-1)x+18=0$ be twice the other. Then the length of the latus rectum of the parabola $y^2=6kx$ is equal to:

steps.text: Let roots be $r,2r$. Sum: $3r=\frac{-9(k-1)}{k^2-15k+27}$, product: $2r^2=\frac{18}{k^2-15k+27}$.

From the sum, $r=\frac{-3(k-1)}{k^2-15k+27}$. Substituting in the product: $\frac{18(k-1)^2}{(k^2-15k+27)^2}=\frac{18}{k^2-15k+27}$, so $(k-1)^2=k^2-15k+27$, giving $13k=26$, i.e. $k=2$ (and $k^2-15k+27=1\ne 0$, so it is genuinely quadratic).
The parabola is $y^2=12x=4(3)x$, so its latus rectum is $4\times 3=12$.

pitfalls: Forgetting to verify $k^2-15k+27\ne 0$ (the equation must remain quadratic).
solution.final_check: $r=-3$: check $3r=-9=-9(1)/1$ and $2r^2=18=18/1$ — consistent with $k=2$.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $e_1$ and $e_2$ be two distinct roots of the equation $x^2-ax+2=0$. Let the sets $\{a\in\mathbb{R}: e_1\text{ and }e_2\text{ are the eccentricities of hyperbolas}\}=(\alpha,\beta)$, and $\{a\in\mathbb{R}: e_1\text{ and }e_2\text{ are the eccentricities of an ellipse and a hyperbola, respectively}\}=(\gamma,\infty)$. Then $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2$ is equal to:

formulas: Both roots $>1$ iff $\Delta>0$, $f(1)>0$, $a/2>1$; one root on each side of $1$ iff $f(1)<0$

steps.text: Both hyperbolas: need $e_1,e_2>1$ (distinct). $\Delta=a^2-8>0$, $f(1)=3-a>0$, and vertex $a/2>1$. With $a>0$ this gives $2\sqrt2<a<3$, so $(\alpha,\beta)=(2\sqrt2,3)$.

Ellipse then hyperbola: need $0<e_1<1<e_2$ (distinct). Product $=2>0$ and $f(1)=3-a<0$ (1 lies strictly between the roots) gives $a>3$; then automatically sum $>0$ so both roots are positive with one below and one above $1$. Hence $(\gamma,\infty)=(3,\infty)$, $\gamma=3$.

pitfalls: For the mixed case, $f(1)<0$ alone (with product $>0$) already forces the roots to straddle $1$ — but one must also confirm $e_1>0$, which follows from sum $a>3>0$.
solution.final_check: At $a=2.9$: roots $\approx 1.03, 1.94$ (both $>1$); at $a=3.5$: roots $\approx 0.69, 2.81$ (straddle $1$) — behaviour matches the intervals.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let the set of all values of $k\in\mathbb{R}$ such that the equation $z(\bar{z}+2+i)+k(2+3i)=0$, $z\in\mathbb{C}$, has at least one solution, be the interval $[\alpha,\beta]$. Then $9(\alpha+\beta)$ is equal to:

formulas: Write $z=x+iy$ and split into real and imaginary parts
A real quadratic has a solution iff its discriminant $\ge 0$

steps.text: With $z=x+iy$: $z(\bar z+2+i)=(x^2+y^2+2x-y)+i(x+2y)$. The equation becomes the system: $x^2+y^2+2x-y+2k=0$ and $x+2y+3k=0$.
From the imaginary part $x=-2y-3k$; substituting in the real part gives $5y^2+(12k-5)y+(9k^2-4k)=0$. A real solution $y$ exists iff $\Delta=(12k-5)^2-20(9k^2-4k)\ge 0$, i.e. $-36k^2-40k+25\ge 0$.
The admissible $k$ form $[\alpha,\beta]$ with $36k^2+40k-25=0$ at the endpoints; hence $\alpha+\beta=-40/36=-10/9$ and $9(\alpha+\beta)=-10$.

pitfalls: Sign errors when expanding $(x+iy)((x+2)+i(1-y))$ — compute real and imaginary parts carefully.
solution.final_check: At $k=-10/9$ (midpoint): $5y^2-\tfrac{55}{3}y+\tfrac{130}{9}=0$ has $\Delta>0$; just outside the endpoints $\Delta<0$ — the interval is exactly right.

subject: mathematics
stem: The sum of the first ten terms of an A.P. is $160$ and the sum of the first two terms of a G.P. is $8$. If the first term of the A.P. is equal to the common ratio of the G.P. and the first term of the G.P. is equal to common difference of the A.P., then the sum of all possible values of the first term of the G.P. is:

steps.text: Let the A.P. have first term $A$, difference $d$; the G.P. have first term $a$, ratio $r$. Given $A=r$ and $a=d$: $\frac{10}{2}(2r+9a)=160$, i.e. $2r+9a=32$, and $a(1+r)=8$.
From $a(1+r)=8$: $r=\frac{8}{a}-1$. Substituting: $2\left(\frac{8}{a}-1\right)+9a=32\Rightarrow 9a^2-34a+16=0$.
The sum of all possible values of $a$ is the sum of the roots $=34/9$ (Vieta) — no need to solve for the individual values.

pitfalls: Trying to find each value of $a$ individually; Vieta gives the sum directly. Also $a=0$ is impossible since $a(1+r)=8$.

subject: mathematics
stem: The number of 4-letter words, with or without meaning, each consisting of two vowels and two consonants that can be formed from the letters of the word INCONSEQUENTIAL, without repeating any letter, is:

formulas: $\binom{n}{r}$ ways to choose, $r!$ ways to arrange
No repetition $\Rightarrow$ all 4 chosen letters are distinct

steps.text: INCONSEQUENTIAL has the distinct letters I, N, C, O, S, E, Q, U, T, A, L: 5 distinct vowels (A, E, I, O, U) and 6 distinct consonants (C, L, N, Q, S, T).
Choose 2 vowels from 5: $\binom{5}{2}=10$; choose 2 consonants from 6: $\binom{6}{2}=15$; arrange the 4 distinct letters: $4!=24$.
Total $=10\times 15\times 24=3600$.

pitfalls: Counting repeated letters (N, E, I occur more than once) as distinct choices — the no-repetition condition means only distinct letters matter.
solution.final_check: Sanity check: $\binom{11}{4}\cdot 4!=7920$ total 4-letter words; the 2V+2C restriction $3600<7920$ is plausible.

subject: mathematics
stem: If the coefficients of the middle terms in the binomial expansions of $(1+ax)^{26}$ and $(1-ax)^{28}$, $a\ne 0$, are equal, then the value of $a$ is:

steps.text: Middle term of $(1+ax)^{26}$ is $T_{14}=\binom{26}{13}(ax)^{13}$, coefficient $\binom{26}{13}a^{13}$. Middle term of $(1-ax)^{28}$ is $T_{15}=\binom{28}{14}(-ax)^{14}$, coefficient $\binom{28}{14}a^{14}$ (the $(-1)^{14}=1$).

pitfalls: Dropping the $(-1)^{14}$ sign (here it is $+1$, but in general the sign of the middle coefficient of $(1-ax)^{2n}$ is $(-1)^n$); also misidentifying the middle term index.

subject: mathematics
stem: A data consists of $20$ observations $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{20}$. If $\sum_{i=1}^{20}(x_i+5)^2=2500$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{20}(x_i-5)^2=100$, then the ratio of mean to standard deviation of this data is:

steps.text: Subtracting: $\sum\big((x_i+5)^2-(x_i-5)^2\big)=2400$, but $(x_i+5)^2-(x_i-5)^2=20x_i$, so $20\sum x_i=2400$, giving mean $\bar x=6$.
$\frac{1}{20}\sum(x_i-5)^2=5=\sigma^2+(\bar x-5)^2=\sigma^2+1$, so $\sigma^2=4$ and $\sigma=2$.
Ratio mean : S.D. $=6:2=3:1$.

pitfalls: Confusing $\sum(x_i-5)^2/20$ with the variance itself — it is the variance only about the mean; the shift $(\bar x-5)^2$ must be subtracted.
solution.final_check: Reconstruct: mean $6$, S.D. $2$ gives $\sum(x_i+5)^2/20 = 4+(11)^2 = 125\Rightarrow 2500$ ✓ and $\sum(x_i-5)^2/20=4+1=5\Rightarrow 100$ ✓.

subject: mathematics
stem: A bag contains $(N+1)$ coins — $N$ fair coins, and one coin with 'Head' on both sides. A coin is selected at random and tossed. If the probability of getting 'Head' is $\frac{9}{16}$, then $N$ is equal to:

steps.text: $P(\text{double-headed coin})=\frac{1}{N+1}$, $P(\text{fair coin})=\frac{N}{N+1}$. So $P(H)=\frac{1}{N+1}\cdot 1+\frac{N}{N+1}\cdot\frac12=\frac{9}{16}$.
Multiplying by $16(N+1)$: $16+8N=9N+9$, so $N=7$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the double-headed coin contributes probability $1$, not $1/2$.
solution.final_check: With $N=7$: $P(H)=\frac18+\frac78\cdot\frac12=\frac18+\frac{7}{16}=\frac{9}{16}$ ✓.

subject: mathematics
stem: If the eccentricity $e$ of the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2}-\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$, passing through $(6,4\sqrt{3})$, satisfies $15(e^2+1)=34e$, then the length of the latus rectum of the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{b^2}-\frac{y^2}{2(a^2+1)}=1$ is:

steps.text: $15e^2-34e+15=0$ gives $e=\frac{34\pm 16}{30}\in\{\frac53,\frac35\}$; for a hyperbola $e>1$, so $e=\frac53$. Then $\frac{b^2}{a^2}=e^2-1=\frac{16}{9}$.
New hyperbola: $\frac{x^2}{16}-\frac{y^2}{20}=1$. Latus rectum $=\frac{2\times 20}{4}=10$.

pitfalls: Picking $e=3/5$ (invalid for a hyperbola) or swapping the transverse/conjugate axes in the new hyperbola when computing the latus rectum.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let chord $PQ$ of length $3\sqrt{13}$ of the parabola $y^2=12x$ be such that the ordinates of points $P$ and $Q$ are in the ratio $1:2$. If the chord $PQ$ subtends an angle $\alpha$ at the focus of the parabola, then $\sin\alpha$ is equal to:

steps.text: Here $4a=12$, $a=3$, focus $S=(3,0)$. Write $P=(3t_1^2,6t_1)$, $Q=(3t_2^2,6t_2)$ with $t_2=2t_1$ (ordinates in ratio $1:2$). Let $t_1=t$.
$\vec{SP}=(0,6t)$, $\vec{SQ}=(9,12t)$: $\cos\alpha=\frac{72t^2}{6|t|\sqrt{81+144t^2}}=\frac{72}{90}=\frac45$, so $\sin\alpha=\frac35$ (positive).

pitfalls: Using the ordinate ratio as $t_1:t_2=1:2$ but then also flipping the sign of one parameter — both points must use the same-signed $t$ for the chord length to work out.
solution.final_check: Focal distances: $SP=6=a+3t_1^2$... $SP=|(0,6)|=6$, $SQ=|(9,12)|=15$; by the law of cosines $PQ^2=36+225-2\cdot6\cdot15\cdot\frac45=117=9\cdot13$ ✓.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $0<\alpha<1$, $\beta=\frac{1}{3\alpha}$ and $\tan^{-1}(1-\alpha)+\tan^{-1}(1-\beta)=\frac{\pi}{4}$. Then $6(\alpha+\beta)$ is equal to:

steps.text: Take $\tan$ of both sides: $\frac{(1-\alpha)+(1-\beta)}{1-(1-\alpha)(1-\beta)}=1$, so $2-(\alpha+\beta)=\alpha+\beta-\alpha\beta$, i.e. $\alpha\beta=2(\alpha+\beta)-2$.
With $\beta=\frac{1}{3\alpha}$: $\alpha\beta=\frac13$, so $\frac13=2(\alpha+\beta)-2$, giving $\alpha+\beta=\frac76$ and $6(\alpha+\beta)=7$.
Consistency: $\{\alpha,\beta\}$ are roots of $t^2-\frac76t+\frac13=0$, i.e. $\{\frac12,\frac23\}$, and $\tan^{-1}\frac13+\tan^{-1}\frac12=\frac\pi4$ indeed (sum in $(0,\pi)$ with $\tan=1$).

pitfalls: Blindly applying $\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\frac{x+y}{1-xy}$ without confirming the sum is $\pi/4$ and not $5\pi/4$ — the range check above rules that out.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $S=\{\theta\in(-2\pi,2\pi):\cos\theta+1=\sqrt{3}\sin\theta\}$. Then $\sum_{\theta\in S}\theta$ is equal to:

steps.text: $\cos\theta-\sqrt3\sin\theta=-1$, i.e. $2\cos\left(\theta+\frac\pi3\right)=-1$, so $\theta+\frac\pi3=\pm\frac{2\pi}{3}+2n\pi$.
Hence $\theta=\frac\pi3+2n\pi$ or $\theta=-\pi+2n\pi$. In $(-2\pi,2\pi)$ these give $\theta\in\{\frac\pi3,-\frac{5\pi}3,-\pi,\pi\}$.
Sum $=\frac\pi3-\frac{5\pi}3-\pi+\pi=-\frac{4\pi}3$.

pitfalls: Losing the $n=-1$ solution $-5\pi/3$ (it lies inside $(-2\pi,2\pi)$) or wrongly including $7\pi/3$.
solution.final_check: Each listed $\theta$ satisfies $\cos\theta+1=\sqrt3\sin\theta$ (e.g. $\theta=\pi$: $0=0$ ✓) and no other values in the interval do.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let the image of the point $P(1,6,a)$ in the line $L:\frac{x}{1}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z-a+1}{b}$, $b>0$, be $\left(\frac{a}{3},0,a+c\right)$. If $S(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$, $\alpha>0$, is the point on $L$ such that the distance of $S$ from the foot of perpendicular from the point $P$ on $L$ is $2\sqrt{14}$, then $\alpha+\beta+\gamma$ is equal to:

concepts: Image of a point in a line
formulas: Midpoint of $P$ and its image lies on the line; $\vec{PQ}$ is perpendicular to the line's direction

steps.text: Midpoint $M=\left(\frac{1+a/3}{2},3,\frac{2a+c}{2}\right)$ lies on $L$: from $x=\frac{y-1}{2}$: $\frac{1+a/3}{2}=1$, so $a=3$.

$\vec{PQ}=(0,-6,c)$ is perpendicular to direction $(1,2,b)$: $-12+bc=0$. Also $M_z=b+2$ gives $\frac{6+c}{2}=b+2$, i.e. $c=2b-2$. With $bc=12$: $b(2b-2)=12\Rightarrow b=3$ ($b>0$), $c=4$. Foot $M=(1,3,5)$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the $b>0$ condition when solving $b^2-b-6=0$ (the root $b=-2$ must be rejected), or picking $t=-1$ which gives $\alpha<0$.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let a line $L$ be perpendicular to both the lines $L_1:\frac{x+1}{3}=\frac{y+3}{5}=\frac{z+5}{7}$ and $L_2:\frac{x-2}{1}=\frac{y-4}{4}=\frac{z-6}{7}$. If $\theta$ is the acute angle between the lines $L$ and $L_3:\frac{x-\frac{8}{7}}{2}=\frac{y-\frac{4}{7}}{1}=\frac{z}{2}$, then $\tan\theta$ is equal to:

steps.text: $\tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt{1-4/54}}{2/(3\sqrt6)}=\frac{5/(3\sqrt3)}{2/(3\sqrt6)}=\frac{5\sqrt2}{2}$.

pitfalls: Using the signed (not absolute) dot product for an acute angle, or arithmetic slips in the cross product.

subject: mathematics
stem: The value of $\lim_{x\to 0}\left(\frac{x^2\sin^2 x}{x^2-\sin^2 x}\right)$ is:

steps.text: Numerator: $x^2\sin^2 x=x^2\left(x^2-\frac{x^4}{3}+O(x^6)\right)=x^4-\frac{x^6}{3}+O(x^8)$.
Denominator: $x^2-\sin^2 x=\frac{x^4}{3}+O(x^6)$.

pitfalls: Applying L'Hôpital mechanically four times is error-prone; the series method is cleaner. Note the denominator's leading term is $x^4/3$, not $x^4$.
solution.final_check: Numerically at $x=0.01$: value $\approx 2.9999$ — converges to $3$.

subject: mathematics
stem: The value of the integral $\int_{-\pi/4}^{\pi/4}\left(\frac{32\cos^4 x}{1+e^{\sin x}}\right)dx$ is:

formulas: $\int_{-a}^{a}\frac{f(x)}{1+e^{g(x)}}dx=\int_{0}^{a}f(x)dx$ when $f$ is even and $g$ is odd

steps.text: Here $f(x)=32\cos^4x$ is even and $g(x)=\sin x$ is odd, so the integral equals $\int_{0}^{\pi/4}32\cos^4x\,dx$.
Integrating $0\to\pi/4$: $12\cdot\frac\pi4+16\cdot\frac{\sin(\pi/2)}{2}+4\cdot\frac{\sin\pi}{4}=3\pi+8+0=3\pi+8$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the hypothesis: the $\int_{-a}^{a}\to\int_0^a$ reduction needs $f$ even AND the exponent odd; also $\int_0^{\pi/4}\cos 4x\,dx=0$ (don't drop it silently).
solution.final_check: Differentiating the antiderivative $12x+8\sin 2x+\sin 4x$ gives $12+16\cos 2x+4\cos 4x$ ✓; at $\pi/4$: $3\pi+8$ ✓.

subject: mathematics
stem: The area of the region $\{(x,y):0\le y\le 6-x,\ y^2\ge 4x-3,\ x\ge 0\}$ is:

formulas: Integrate $x$ as a function of $y$ between intersection points

steps.text: The line $y=6-x$ meets the parabola $x=\frac{y^2+3}{4}$ at $6-y=\frac{y^2+3}{4}$, i.e. $y^2+4y-21=0$, so $(y+7)(y-3)=0$; with $y\ge 0$: $y=3$, $x=3$.
For $0\le y\le 3$ the binding constraint is the parabola ($x\le\frac{y^2+3}{4}<6-y$); for $3\le y\le 6$ it is the line ($x\le 6-y$).

pitfalls: Integrating with respect to $x$ without splitting at the intersection, or misreading $y^2\ge 4x-3$ as the region above the parabola in $y$ (for fixed $y$ it is $x$ that is bounded).
solution.final_check: At $y=0$: allowed $x\in[0,3/4]$ (parabola) ✓; at $y=5$: allowed $x\in[0,1]$ (line) ✓; triangle part has area $\frac12\cdot 3\cdot 3=4.5$ ✓.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $e$ be the base of natural logarithm and let $f:\{1,2,3,4\}\to\{1,e,e^2,e^3\}$ and $g:\{1,e,e^2,e^3\}\to\left\{1,\frac12,\frac13,\frac14\right\}$ be two bijective functions such that $f$ is strictly decreasing and $g$ is strictly increasing. If $\phi(x)=\left[f^{-1}\left\{g^{-1}\left(\frac12\right)\right\}\right]^x$, then the area of the region $R=\{(x,y):x^2\le y\le\phi(x),\ 0\le x\le 1\}$ is:

formulas: Strictly increasing bijection maps ordered domain to ordered codomain

steps.text: $f$ strictly decreasing: $f(1)=e^3,f(2)=e^2,f(3)=e,f(4)=1$. $g$ strictly increasing: $g(1)=\frac14,g(e)=\frac13,g(e^2)=\frac12,g(e^3)=1$.
Hence $g^{-1}(1/2)=e^2$ and $f^{-1}(e^2)=2$, so $\phi(x)=2^x$. On $[0,1]$, $2^x\ge 1\ge x^2$, so the region is valid throughout.
Area $=\int_0^1(2^x-x^2)dx=\left[\frac{2^x}{\ln 2}-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1=\frac{1}{\ln 2}-\frac13=\frac{3-\ln 2}{3\ln 2}$.

pitfalls: Mapping $g$ backwards: 'strictly increasing' means the smallest domain value takes the smallest codomain value ($g(1)=1/4$, not $1$). Also the exponent in $\phi$ is $+x$, giving $2^x\ge x^2$ on $[0,1]$ — with $2^{-x}$ the region would be empty near $x=1$.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & -1\\ 1 & 0 & 1\\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}$ satisfy $A^2+\alpha\big(\mathrm{adj}(\mathrm{adj}(A))\big)+\beta\big(\mathrm{adj}(A)\big)\big(\mathrm{adj}(\mathrm{adj}(A))\big)=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -2 & 2\\ -2 & 0 & -1\\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}$ for some $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}$. Then $(\alpha-\beta)^2$ is equal to ______.

steps.text: $|A|=-1\cdot(0-0)-1\cdot(1-0)+(-1)\cdot 0=-1$. For $3\times 3$: $\mathrm{adj}(\mathrm{adj}(A))=|A|A=-A$.
$\big(\mathrm{adj}(A)\big)\big(\mathrm{adj}(\mathrm{adj}(A))\big)=\mathrm{adj}(A)\cdot(|A|A)=|A|^2I=I$.

So $A^2-\alpha A+\beta I=\begin{bmatrix}2&-2&2\\-2&0&-1\\0&0&-1\end{bmatrix}$. With $A^2=\begin{bmatrix}2&-1&1\\-1&1&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}$: entry $(1,2)$ gives $-1-\alpha=-2$, so $\alpha=1$; entry $(2,2)$ gives $1+\beta=0$, so $\beta=-1$. All other entries check out.

pitfalls: Using $\mathrm{adj}(\mathrm{adj}(A))=|A|^{n-1}A$ (wrong exponent) — for $n=3$ it is $|A|^{1}A$.
solution.final_check: With $\alpha=1,\beta=-1$: $A^2-A-I=\begin{bmatrix}2&-2&2\\-2&0&-1\\0&0&-1\end{bmatrix}$ entry-by-entry ✓ (verified numerically).

subject: mathematics
stem: Let the centre of the circle $x^2+y^2+2gx+2fy+25=0$ be in the first quadrant and lie on the line $2x-y=4$. Let the area of an equilateral triangle inscribed in the circle be $27\sqrt{3}$. Then the square of the length of the chord of the circle on the line $x=1$ is ______.

formulas: Chord length $=2\sqrt{R^2-d^2}$ where $d$ is the centre-to-line distance

steps.text: Area $27\sqrt3=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}s^2$ gives $s^2=108$, $s=6\sqrt3$; inscribed equilateral triangle has $s=R\sqrt3$, so $R=6$.
Distance from $(5,6)$ to $x=1$ is $4$; half-chord $=\sqrt{36-16}=2\sqrt5$; chord $=4\sqrt5$; its square $=80$.

pitfalls: Taking the wrong root $g=1.8$ (centre must be in the first quadrant) or forgetting to square the chord length.

subject: mathematics
stem: If $\vec{a}=\hat{i}+\hat{j}+\hat{k}$, $\vec{b}=\hat{j}-\hat{k}$ and $\vec{c}$ be three vectors such that $\vec{a}\times\vec{c}=\vec{b}$ and $\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=3$, then $\vec{c}\cdot(\vec{a}-2\vec{b})$ is equal to ______.

steps.text: Let $\vec c=(x,y,z)$. $\vec a\times\vec c=(z-y,x-z,y-x)=(0,1,-1)$ gives $z=y$, $x=1+z$, $y=x-1$ (consistent).
$\vec a\cdot\vec c=x+y+z=3$ gives $(1+z)+z+z=3$, so $z=\frac23$, $x=\frac53$, $y=\frac23$.
$\vec c\cdot(\vec a-2\vec b)=\vec c\cdot\vec a-2\,\vec c\cdot\vec b=3-2\left(0+\frac23-\frac23\right)=3$.

pitfalls: Solving the cross-product system inconsistently — the three scalar equations are dependent, so the dot-product condition is needed to fix $\vec c$.

subject: mathematics
stem: For the functions $f(\theta)=\alpha\tan^2\theta+\beta\cot^2\theta$ and $g(\theta)=\alpha\sin^2\theta+\beta\cos^2\theta$, $\alpha>\beta>0$, let $\min_{0<\theta<\pi/2}f(\theta)=\max_{0<\theta<\pi}g(\theta)$. If the first term of a G.P. is $\left(\frac{\alpha}{2\beta}\right)$, its common ratio is $\left(\frac{2\beta}{\alpha}\right)$ and the sum of its first $10$ terms is $\frac{m}{n}$, $\gcd(m,n)=1$, then $m+n$ is equal to ______.

steps.text: $\min_{0<\theta<\pi/2}f(\theta)=2\sqrt{\alpha\beta}$ (attained when $\alpha\tan^2\theta=\beta\cot^2\theta$). $g(\theta)=\beta+(\alpha-\beta)\sin^2\theta$ is maximised at $\sin^2\theta=1$ ($\theta=\pi/2\in(0,\pi)$), giving $\max g=\alpha$.
Equality: $2\sqrt{\alpha\beta}=\alpha\Rightarrow\alpha=4\beta$ (using $\alpha>0$).

pitfalls: Assuming $\max g$ occurs at an endpoint — $\sin^2\theta$ attains $1$ inside $(0,\pi)$, so the maximum is $\alpha$, not a limit value.

subject: mathematics
stem: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $(x^2-x\sqrt{x^2-1})dy+(y(x-\sqrt{x^2-1})-x)dx=0$, $x\ge 1$. If $y(1)=1$, then the greatest integer less than $y(\sqrt{5})$ is ______.

steps.text: $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{x-y(x-\sqrt{x^2-1})}{x(x-\sqrt{x^2-1})}=\frac{1}{x-\sqrt{x^2-1}}-\frac{y}{x}=(x+\sqrt{x^2-1})-\frac{y}{x}$.
Linear form: $\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{1}{x}y=x+\sqrt{x^2-1}$ with I.F. $x$: $\frac{d}{dx}(xy)=x^2+x\sqrt{x^2-1}$.
At $x=\sqrt5$: $\sqrt5\,y=\frac{5\sqrt5}{3}+\frac{8}{3}+\frac23=\frac{5\sqrt5+10}{3}$, so $y(\sqrt5)=\frac{5+2\sqrt5}{3}\approx 3.157$. Greatest integer less than it: $3$.

pitfalls: Algebra slip in rationalising $1/(x-\sqrt{x^2-1})$ — multiply by the conjugate; the denominator becomes $x^2-(x^2-1)=1$. Also $\int x\sqrt{x^2-1}dx=\frac{(x^2-1)^{3/2}}{3}$ (substitute $u=x^2-1$).
solution.final_check: Check: differentiating $xy=\frac{x^3+(x^2-1)^{3/2}+2}{3}$ gives $y+x\frac{dy}{dx}=x^2+x\sqrt{x^2-1}$ ✓; $y(\sqrt5)=(5+2\sqrt5)/3\approx 3.1574$, strictly between $3$ and $4$ ✓.

subject: physics
stem: The density $\rho$ of a uniform cylinder is determined by measuring its mass $m$, length $l$ and diameter $d$. The measured values of $m$, $l$ and $d$ are $97.42 \pm 0.02$ g, $8.35 \pm 0.05$ mm and $20.20 \pm 0.02$ mm, respectively. Calculated percentage fractional error in $\rho$ is ______.

steps.text: Density of the cylinder: $\rho = \dfrac{m}{\pi d^2 l / 4} = \dfrac{4m}{\pi d^2 l}$, so $\rho \propto m^1 d^{-2} l^{-1}$.
For products/powers, fractional errors add with the power as multiplier: $\dfrac{\Delta\rho}{\rho} = \dfrac{\Delta m}{m} + 2\dfrac{\Delta d}{d} + \dfrac{\Delta l}{l}$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the factor 2 on the diameter term (since $d$ appears squared).
Mixing up which error belongs to $l$ and $d$ — the values are listed in the order $m, l, d$.
solution.final_check: Largest contribution is from the length measurement ($0.60\%$); total $0.82\%$ matches option B.

subject: physics
stem: The potential energy of a particle changes with distance $x$ from a fixed origin as $V = \dfrac{A\sqrt{x}}{x + B}$, where $A$ and $B$ are constant with appropriate dimensions. The dimensions of $AB$ are ______.

steps.text: $V$ is an energy, so $[V] = ML^2T^{-2}$.
In the denominator $x + B$, only like dimensions can be added, so $[B] = [x] = L$.
$[AB] = ML^{5/2}T^{-2}\cdot L = ML^{7/2}T^{-2}$, which is option D.

pitfalls: Treating $[\sqrt{x}]$ as dimensionless instead of $L^{1/2}$.
solution.final_check: Dimensions multiply cleanly: $A$ carries $L^{5/2}$ and $B$ carries $L$, giving $L^{7/2}$ as in option D.

subject: physics
stem: The rain drop of mass 1 g, starts with zero velocity from a height of 1 km. It hits the ground with a speed of 5 m/s. The work done by the unknown resistive force is ______ J. (take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)

steps.text: By the work-energy theorem, the work of gravity plus the work of the resistive force equals the change in kinetic energy: $mgh + W_r = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0$.
Final kinetic energy: $\tfrac{1}{2}\times 10^{-3}\times 25 = 0.0125$ J.
$W_r = 0.0125 - 10 = -9.9875$ J $\approx -9.99$ J, closest to option D ($-9.98$). The negative sign shows the resistive force opposes the motion.

pitfalls: Using $m = 1$ kg instead of $10^{-3}$ kg.
Dropping the small final KE term — here it only shifts the second decimal, but it must be included.
solution.final_check: $|W_r| = 9.9875 \approx 10$ J, i.e. nearly all the gravitational work is dissipated, consistent with a tiny impact speed; option D is the only match.

subject: physics
stem:
Two blocks ($P$ and $Q$) with respectively masses 2 kg and 1.5 kg are joined by a massless thread. These blocks are mounted on a frictionless pulley which is fixed on the edge of a cube ($S$), as shown in the figure. Block $P$ is positioned on the top surface which has no friction and block $Q$ is in contact with side-surface, having coefficient friction $\mu$. The cube ($S$) moves towards the right with acceleration of $\dfrac{g}{2}$, where $g$ is gravitational acceleration. During this movement the block $P$ and $Q$ remain stationary. The value of $\mu$ is ______. (take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$)
[Figure: cube $S$; block $P$ (2 kg) rests on the top face, joined by a horizontal thread passing over a pulley fixed at the top-right edge; block $Q$ (1.5 kg) hangs vertically against the right side face of the cube.]

formulas: $T = m_P a$ (block $P$ in the cube's frame)
$f = m_Q g - T$, $N = m_Q a$, $\mu N \ge f$

steps.text: Work in the cube's (non-inertial) frame, accelerating right at $a = g/2$. Each block feels a pseudo-force $ma$ to the left.
Block $P$ (2 kg) on the frictionless top: the thread tension balances its pseudo-force, so $T = m_P a = 2\times \dfrac{g}{2} = g = 10$ N.
Block $Q$ (1.5 kg) hangs against the side wall: the pseudo-force presses it against the wall, giving normal reaction $N = m_Q a = 1.5\times 5 = 7.5$ N.
Vertically on $Q$: $T + f = m_Q g$, so friction $f = 15 - 10 = 5$ N upward. For no slipping, $\mu N \ge f$, i.e. $\mu \ge \dfrac{5}{7.5} = \dfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.67$.
The minimum $\mu$ that keeps $Q$ stationary is $0.67$, option B.

pitfalls: Using $N = m_Q g$ (wrong — the normal comes from the horizontal pseudo-force, not weight).
Forgetting that the thread tension is set by block $P$'s pseudo-force.
solution.final_check: Friction needed is $5$ N against a normal of $7.5$ N, so $\mu = 2/3 \approx 0.67$, matching option B.

subject: physics
stem: A lift of mass 1600 kg is supported by thick iron wire. If the maximum stress which the wire can withstand is $4 \times 10^8$ N/m$^2$ and its radius is 4 mm, then maximum acceleration the lift can take is ______ m/s$^2$. (take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$ and $\pi = 3.14$)

concepts: Newton's second law for a lift

steps.text: Maximum tension the wire can bear: $T_{max} = \sigma_{max}A = (4\times 10^8)\times \pi(4\times 10^{-3})^2 = 4\times 10^8\times 3.14\times 16\times 10^{-6} = 20096$ N.
For the lift accelerating upward with acceleration $a$, tension $T = m(g+a)$.

pitfalls: Using diameter instead of radius in the area.
Forgetting to add $g$ — the wire also supports the lift's weight.
solution.final_check: $T_{max}/m = 12.56$ m/s$^2$ exceeds $g$ by $2.56$ m/s$^2$, the allowed upward acceleration — option A.

subject: physics
stem: A solid sphere of radius 4 cm and mass 5 kg is rotating (rotation axis is passing through the centre of the sphere) with an angular velocity of 1200 rpm. It is brought to rest in 10 s by applying a constant torque. The torque applied and the number of rotations it made before it comes to rest are ______ and ______ respectively.

steps.text: Initial angular speed: $\omega_0 = 1200\,\text{rpm} = \dfrac{1200\times 2\pi}{60} = 40\pi$ rad/s.
Moment of inertia of the solid sphere: $I = \dfrac{2}{5}\times 5\times (0.04)^2 = 2\times 1.6\times 10^{-3} = 3.2\times 10^{-3}$ kg m$^2$.
Angular deceleration: $\alpha = \dfrac{40\pi}{10} = 4\pi$ rad/s$^2$. Torque $\tau = I\alpha = 3.2\times 10^{-3}\times 4\pi = 0.0128\pi$ N m.
Angle turned before stopping: $\theta = \dfrac{\omega_0 + 0}{2}t = \dfrac{40\pi\times 10}{2} = 200\pi$ rad, i.e. $N = \dfrac{200\pi}{2\pi} = 100$ rotations.
Hence $0.0128\pi$ Nm and 100 rotations — option D.

pitfalls: Using $R = 4$ m instead of $0.04$ m.
Confusing rpm with rad/s.
solution.final_check: $\tau = 0.0128\pi$ with $100$ full turns is exactly option D; the $0.128\pi$ options are off by a factor of 10.

subject: physics
stem:
A smooth inclined plane ends in a vertical circular loop, as shown in the figure. A small body is released from height $h$ as shown. If the body exerts a force of three times its weight on the plane at the highest point of circle then the height $h = \alpha R$. The value of $\alpha$ is ______.
[Figure: a smooth incline descending from height $h$ on the left, joining a vertical circular loop of radius $R$ on the right.]

steps.text: The body presses the track with $3mg$ at the top, so the track pushes back on the body with normal $N = 3mg$ downward.
Radial equation at the top: $N + mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$, i.e. $4mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{R}$, so $v^2 = 4gR$ at the top.
Energy conservation from release to the top (smooth plane, no friction): $mgh = mg(2R) + \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = 2mgR + 2mgR = 4mgR$.
Thus $h = 4R$, so $\alpha = 4$, option B.

pitfalls: Writing $N = mv^2/R$ without adding $mg$ (both act downward at the top).
Using the height of the top as $R$ instead of $2R$.
solution.final_check: $v^2 = 4gR$ at the top needs $4mgR$ of initial potential energy, i.e. $h = 4R$ — option B.

subject: physics
stem:
The position of center of mass of three masses 2 kg, 3 kg and 15 kg placed with respect to mid point ($p$) of normal bisector, as shown in the figure is ______.
[Figure: triangle with 15 kg at the top vertex and 2 kg, 3 kg at the base vertices (2 kg on the left); each equal side is 10 m; vertex angle $120^\circ$; a dashed altitude is drawn from the 15 kg vertex to the midpoint of the base; $p$ is the midpoint of this dashed altitude.]

concepts: Centre of mass of a system of particles
formulas: $x_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_i x_i}{\sum m_i}$, $y_{cm} = \dfrac{\sum m_i y_i}{\sum m_i}$

steps.text: Altitude of the triangle from the $120^\circ$ vertex: $10\cos 60^\circ = 5$ m; half-base $= 10\sin 60^\circ = 5\sqrt{3}$ m.
Put $p$ (midpoint of the altitude) at the origin with the altitude along $y$: 15 kg at $(0, +2.5)$, 2 kg at $(-5\sqrt{3}, -2.5)$, 3 kg at $(+5\sqrt{3}, -2.5)$ (metres).
The CM is at $(\sqrt{3}/4,\ 1.25)$ relative to $p$ — option A.

pitfalls: Measuring coordinates from the vertex or base instead of from $p$.
Sign errors on the base masses' $y$-coordinates.
solution.final_check: The heavy 15 kg mass pulls the CM above $p$ ($y = +1.25$) and the 3 kg mass shifts it right ($x = +\sqrt{3}/4$), exactly option A.

subject: physics
stem: The two wires $A$ and $B$ of equal cross-section but of different materials are joined together. The ratio of Young's modulus of wire $A$ and wire $B$ is 20/11. When the joined wire is kept under certain tension the elongations in the wires $A$ and $B$ are equal. If the length of wire $A$ is 2.2 m, then the length of wire $B$ is ______ m.

steps.text: For each wire, elongation $\Delta L = \dfrac{FL}{AY}$. The joined wire carries the same tension $F$ in both, and the cross-sections $A$ are equal.
Equal elongations: $\dfrac{FL_A}{AY_A} = \dfrac{FL_B}{AY_B}$, so $\dfrac{L_A}{Y_A} = \dfrac{L_B}{Y_B}$.
$L_B = L_A\cdot \dfrac{Y_B}{Y_A} = 2.2\times \dfrac{11}{20} = 2.2\times 0.55 = 1.21$ m — option C.

pitfalls: Inverting the modulus ratio (using $Y_A/Y_B$ instead of $Y_B/Y_A$).
solution.final_check: $L_B$ scales with $1/Y$: wire $B$ is softer ($Y_B < Y_A$), so it must be shorter — $1.21$ m $< 2.2$ m, option C.

subject: physics
stem: Two closed vessels of same volume are joined through a narrow tube and both vessels are filled with air of pressure 90 kPa and temperature 400 K. Keeping the temperature of one vessel constant at 400 K the second vessel temperature is raised to 500 K. The final pressure in the vessels is ______ kPa.

steps.text: The joined vessels reach a common final pressure $p$. Let each vessel have volume $V$. Total moles are conserved.
Initially: $n_{total} = 2\times \dfrac{90V}{R\times 400}$.
Finally: $n_{total} = \dfrac{pV}{R\times 400} + \dfrac{pV}{R\times 500}$.
Equating: $p\left(\dfrac{1}{400}+\dfrac{1}{500}\right) = \dfrac{180}{400}$, so $p\cdot \dfrac{9}{2000} = \dfrac{180}{400}$, giving $p = \dfrac{180\times 2000}{400\times 9} = 100$ kPa — option A.

pitfalls: Assuming the pressure stays 90 kPa (it must rise since one vessel is heated at constant volume).
Using $p \propto T$ on the heated vessel alone, ignoring gas redistribution through the tube.
solution.final_check: Heating one vessel drives gas into the other; the common pressure $100$ kPa lies between $90$ and $112.5$ kPa, as expected — option A.

subject: physics
stem: In interference experiment the path difference between two interfering waves at a point $A$ on the screen is $\lambda/3$, where $\lambda$ is the wavelength of these waves, and at another point $B$ the path difference is $\lambda/6$. The ratio of intensities at points $A$ and $B$ is ______.

steps.text: Phase differences: at $A$, $\phi_A = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\cdot\dfrac{\lambda}{3} = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}$; at $B$, $\phi_B = \dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\cdot\dfrac{\lambda}{6} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$.
For two equal-intensity waves ($I_0$ each): $I_A = 2I_0(1+\cos 2\pi/3) = 2I_0(1-\tfrac{1}{2}) = I_0$.
Ratio $\dfrac{I_A}{I_B} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ — option C.

pitfalls: Using the path difference directly as the phase (forgetting the $2\pi/\lambda$ factor).
Reversing the ratio (answering $I_B/I_A = 3$).
solution.final_check: Point $A$ is closer to destructive interference ($\phi = 120^\circ$) so $I_A < I_B$; the ratio $1/3$ (option C) reflects that.

subject: physics
stem: A particle is executing simple harmonic motion. Its amplitude is $A$ and time period is 5 sec. The time required by it to move from $x = A$ to $x = \dfrac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$ is ______ sec.

steps.text: Take $t = 0$ when the particle is at the extreme $x = A$: $x(t) = A\cos(\omega t)$ with $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{5}$ rad/s.
Set $x = \dfrac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$: $\cos(\omega t) = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, so $\omega t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
$t = \dfrac{\pi/4}{2\pi/5} = \dfrac{\pi}{4}\times \dfrac{5}{2\pi} = \dfrac{5}{8}$ s — option C.

pitfalls: Using $x = A\sin(\omega t)$, which shifts the time origin.
Answering the time from mean position instead of from the extreme.
solution.final_check: $5/8$ s is one-eighth of the period, matching the $45^\circ$ phase change on the reference circle — option C.

subject: physics
stem: A thin half ring of radius 35 cm is uniformly charged with a total charge of $Q$ coulomb. If the magnitude of the electric field at centre of the half ring is 100 V/m, then the value of $Q$ is ______ nC. ($\epsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ C$^2$/Nm$^2$ and $\pi = 3.14$)

concepts: Electric field of a charged arc

steps.text: Linear charge density: $\lambda = \dfrac{Q}{\pi R}$ (charge spread over the semicircular arc of length $\pi R$).
Field at the centre of a half ring (components along the arc cancel pairwise, perpendicular components add): $E = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{R} = \dfrac{2kQ}{\pi R^2}$.
$Q = \dfrac{E\pi R^2}{2k} = E\pi R^2\cdot 2\pi\epsilon_0 = 100\times 3.14\times (0.35)^2\times 2\times 3.14\times 8.85\times 10^{-12}$.
$Q = 2.14\times 10^{-9}$ C $= 2.14$ nC — option A.

pitfalls: Using the full-ring result ($E = 0$) or the quarter-ring factor.
Putting $R = 35$ m instead of $0.35$ m.
solution.final_check: $E \propto Q/R^2$: with $R = 0.35$ m and $E = 100$ V/m the charge must be a few nC, and $2.14$ nC (option A) is the computed value.

subject: physics
stem:
The maximum rated power of the LED is 2 mW and it is used in the circuit with input voltage of 5 V as shown in the figure below. The current through resistance $R_S$ is 0.5 mA. The minimum value of the resistance of $R_S$, to ensure that the LED is not damaged is ______ k$\Omega$.
[Figure: 5 V battery; the top lead goes through $R_S$ to a node that splits into two parallel branches to the bottom rail: (i) $R = 1$ k$\Omega$ in series with a reverse-biased protection diode (no current in normal operation), (ii) the 2 mW LED in the forward direction.]

steps.text: The protection diode branch is reverse-biased, so the entire 0.5 mA through $R_S$ flows through the LED.
The LED is safe while $P_{LED} = V_{LED}\times 0.5\,\text{mA} \le 2$ mW, i.e. $V_{LED} \le \dfrac{2\times 10^{-3}}{0.5\times 10^{-3}} = 4$ V.
KVL around the loop: $5 = I R_S + V_{LED}$, so $IR_S = 5 - V_{LED} \ge 1$ V.
$R_S \ge \dfrac{1}{0.5\times 10^{-3}} = 2000\,\Omega = 2$ k$\Omega$. The minimum safe value is 2 k$\Omega$ — option B.

pitfalls: Ignoring the LED power rating and using only Ohm's law with an assumed LED voltage.
Thinking the parallel $R$ + diode branch draws current (it is reverse-biased).
solution.final_check: At $R_S = 2$ k$\Omega$ the LED sees exactly $4$ V $\times 0.5$ mA $= 2$ mW, its rated maximum — option B.

subject: physics
stem: A point light source emits E.M. waves in free space. A detector, placed at a distance of $L$ m, measures the intensity as $I_0$. The detector is now shifted to another location on the same spherical surface ensuring the angle between original location and new location as $45^\circ$. The measured intensity at new location will be ______.

formulas: $I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2}$ for an isotropic point source

steps.text: A point source radiates uniformly in all directions in free space, so the intensity at distance $r$ is $I = \dfrac{P}{4\pi r^2}$, depending only on $r$.
The new location lies on the same spherical surface of radius $L$, so $r = L$ is unchanged and the measured intensity is still $I_0$.
The $45^\circ$ angle between the two locations is a distractor — it does not enter the inverse-square law. Answer: $I_0$, option B.

pitfalls: Misapplying Malus's law ($I_0\cos^2 45^\circ = I_0/2$) — there is no polarizer here.
Confusing angular position with distance from the source.
solution.final_check: Same sphere, same distance, same intensity: $I_0$ (option B); the angle is irrelevant for an isotropic radiator.

subject: physics
stem:
A spherical interface lens of radius $R$ separates two media of refractive indices 1 and 1.4 respectively as shown in the figure below. A point source is placed at a distance of $4R$ in front of spherical interface. The magnitude of the magnification of point source image is ______.
[Figure: point object $p$ on the optical axis in medium $n_1 = 1$, at distance $4R$ from a spherical refracting surface of radius $R$; the surface is concave toward the object, with its centre of curvature lying in medium $n_2 = 1.4$.]

steps.text: Cartesian sign convention (light travels left to right): object distance $u = -4R$; centre of curvature is on the refracted side, so $R_{surface} = +R$.
$\dfrac{1.4}{v} = \dfrac{0.15}{R}$, so $v = \dfrac{1.4R}{0.15} = \dfrac{28R}{3} \approx 9.33R$ (real image in the denser medium).
Magnification $m = -\dfrac{1\times (28R/3)}{1.4\times (-4R)} = \dfrac{28}{16.8} \approx 1.667$. Magnitude $\approx 1.66$ — option A.

pitfalls: Taking $R$ negative (the surface is concave toward the incident light, but the centre is on the refracted side, so $R > 0$).
Using the mirror magnification formula $m = -v/u$ without the refractive-index factors.
solution.final_check: $v \approx 9.33R$ is a real image and $|m| = v/(1.4\times 4R)\times ... = 1.667 \approx 1.66$, option A.

subject: physics
stem: A small cube of side 1 mm is placed at the centre of a circular loop of radius 10 cm carrying a current of 2 A. The magnetic energy stored inside the cube is $\alpha \times 10^{-14}$ J. The value of $\alpha$ is ______. ($\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}$ Tm/A, $\pi = 3.14$)

concepts: Magnetic field at the centre of a loop

steps.text: Field at the centre of the loop: $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2R} = \dfrac{4\pi\times 10^{-7}\times 2}{2\times 0.1} = 4\pi\times 10^{-6}$ T. The cube is tiny, so $B$ is effectively uniform inside it.
Energy density: $u = \dfrac{B^2}{2\mu_0} = \dfrac{(4\pi\times 10^{-6})^2}{2\times 4\pi\times 10^{-7}} = 2\pi\times 10^{-5}$ J/m$^3$.
$U = 2\pi\times 10^{-5}\times 10^{-9} = 2\pi\times 10^{-14}$ J $= 6.28\times 10^{-14}$ J, so $\alpha = 6.28$ — option A.

pitfalls: Using the loop radius instead of the cube side for the volume.
Writing energy density as $B^2/\mu_0$ (missing the factor $1/2$).
solution.final_check: $U = (B^2/2\mu_0)V = 2\pi\times 10^{-14}$ J gives $\alpha = 2\pi = 6.28$, option A.

subject: physics
stem:
An inductor of inductance 10 mH having resistance of 100 $\Omega$ is connected to battery of E.M.F. 1.0 V through a switch as shown in the figure below. After switch is closed, the ratio of instantaneous voltages across the inductor when the current passing through it is 2 mA and 4 mA is ______.
[Figure: a series loop containing the 10 mH inductor (with 100 $\Omega$ resistance), a 1.0 V battery and a switch.]

concepts: Growth of current in an LR circuit

steps.text: KVL for the charging LR circuit: $E = iR + L\,\dfrac{di}{dt}$, where $R$ is the inductor's own resistance. The voltage across the (ideal) inductive part is $V_L = L\,\dfrac{di}{dt} = E - iR$.
Ratio $= \dfrac{0.8}{0.6} = \dfrac{4}{3}$ — option A.

pitfalls: Using the total voltage $E$ instead of the inductor's share $E - iR$.
Confusing the resistive drop with the inductive voltage.
solution.final_check: As current rises, more of the 1 V drops across the resistance and less across the inductance: $0.8$ V then $0.6$ V, ratio $4/3$ (option A).

subject: physics
stem: The ratio of momentum of the photons of the 1st and 2nd line of Balmer series of Hydrogen atoms is $\alpha/\beta$. The possible values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are:-

steps.text: Balmer series: transitions to $n = 2$. The 1st line is $3\to 2$ and the 2nd line is $4\to 2$.
Photon momentum $p = E/c \propto \left(\dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{n^2}\right)$.
$p_1 \propto \dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{9} = \dfrac{5}{36}$; $p_2 \propto \dfrac{1}{4}-\dfrac{1}{16} = \dfrac{3}{16}$.
$\dfrac{p_1}{p_2} = \dfrac{5/36}{3/16} = \dfrac{5\times 16}{36\times 3} = \dfrac{80}{108} = \dfrac{20}{27}$, so $\alpha = 20$, $\beta = 27$ — option D.

pitfalls: Mixing up the order (1st line is $3	o 2$, not $2	o 1$).
Using wavelength ratio instead of energy/momentum ratio.
solution.final_check: $p_1/p_2 = 20/27 < 1$, consistent with the 1st Balmer line being lower energy than the 2nd — option D.

subject: physics
stem: A LCR series circuit driven with $E_{rms} = 90$ V at frequency $f_d = 30$ Hz has resistance $R = 80$ $\Omega$, an inductance with inductive reactance $X_L = 20.0$ $\Omega$ and capacitance with capacitive reactance $X_C = 80.0$ $\Omega$. The power factor of the circuit is ______.

steps.text: Net reactance: $X = X_L - X_C = 20 - 80 = -60$ $\Omega$ (capacitive).
Power factor $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{80}{100} = 0.8$ — option A.

pitfalls: Using $X_L + X_C$ instead of $X_L - X_C$.
Forgetting to take the square root for $Z$.
solution.final_check: $R:Z = 80:100$ is a 3-4-5 triangle scaled by 20, so $\cos\phi = 0.8$ exactly — option A.

subject: physics
stem:
Refer to the circuit diagram given below. The heat generated across the 6 $\Omega$ resistance in 100 second is $\dfrac{\alpha}{100}$ J. The value of $\alpha$ is ______. (Nearest integer)
[Figure: a 2 V battery whose left (long, positive) plate connects through a 3 $\Omega$ resistor to node $A$, and whose right (short, negative) plate connects to the common right rail; node $A$ connects to the right rail through a 4 $\Omega$ resistor and through a top branch consisting of a 6 $\Omega$ resistor in series with a 3 V battery whose positive (long) plate faces the 6 $\Omega$ resistor.]

steps.text: Battery polarities (long plate = positive): the 2 V battery has $+$ on the left (node $C$), $-$ on the right rail ($X$), so $V_C = V_X + 2$; the 3 V battery has $+$ toward the 6 $\Omega$ resistor (node $D$), so $V_D = V_X + 3$.
Let $u = V_A - V_X$. KCL at $A$: $\dfrac{u-2}{3} + \dfrac{u}{4} + \dfrac{u-3}{6} = 0$ (currents through 3 $\Omega$, 4 $\Omega$ and 6 $\Omega$ branches).
Multiplying by 12: $4(u-2) + 3u + 2(u-3) = 0$, giving $9u = 14$, i.e. $u = 14/9$ V.
Current through the 6 $\Omega$ resistor: $i_6 = \dfrac{V_D - V_A}{6} = \dfrac{3-u}{6} = \dfrac{13/9}{6} = \dfrac{13}{54}$ A.

Heat in 100 s: $H = i_6^2\times 6\times 100 = \left(\dfrac{13}{54}\right)^2\times 600 = \dfrac{8450}{243} \approx 34.774$ J $= \dfrac{\alpha}{100}$, so $\alpha \approx 3477.4$, nearest integer $3477$.

pitfalls: Reversing a battery polarity (the long plate is positive — verified from the diagram).
Writing KCL with inconsistent sign conventions.
solution.final_check: KCL check: $0.389$ A leaves $A$ through 4 $\Omega$ while $0.148 + 0.241 = 0.389$ A enters from the 3 $\Omega$ and 6 $\Omega$ branches — balanced; $\alpha = 3477$.

stem: An unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ passes through polarizer and then through a certain optically active solution and finally it goes to analyser. If the angle between analyser and polariser is $0^\circ$ and intensity of light emerged from analyser is $\dfrac{3}{8}I_0$, the angle of rotation of the light by the solution with respect to analyser is ______ degrees.

steps.text: Unpolarized light of intensity $I_0$ becomes plane-polarized with intensity $I_0/2$ after the polarizer.
The optically active solution rotates the plane of polarization by an angle $\theta$; the analyser axis is at $0^\circ$ to the polarizer, so the light meets the analyser at angle $\theta$.
Malus's law: $I_{out} = \dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{3}{8}I_0$.
$\cos^2\theta = \dfrac{3}{4}$, so $\cos\theta = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\theta = 30^\circ$.

pitfalls: Forgetting the factor $1/2$ from the first polarizer.
Taking $	heta$ from the polarizer instead of the analyser (here both give the same angle since they are aligned).
solution.final_check: $(I_0/2)\cos^2 30^\circ = (I_0/2)(3/4) = 3I_0/8$ — matches the given output intensity, so $30^\circ$ is correct.

stem: The energy released when $\dfrac{7}{17.13}$ kg of $^{7}_{3}$Li is converted into $^{4}_{2}$He by proton bombardment is $\alpha \times 10^{32}$ eV. The value of $\alpha$ is ______. (Nearest integer) (Mass of $^{7}_{3}$Li = 7.0183 u, mass of $^{4}_{2}$He = 4.004 u, mass of proton = 1.008 u and 1 u = 931 MeV/c$^2$ and Avogadro number = $6.0 \times 10^{23}$)

steps.text: Reaction: $^{7}_{3}$Li $+ p \to$ 2$\times^{4}_{2}$He (charge $3+1 = 4$ and mass number $7+1 = 8$ balance).
Energy per reaction: $0.0183\times 931 = 17.037$ MeV.
Total energy $= 3.493\times 10^{25}\times 17.037$ MeV $= 5.952\times 10^{26}$ MeV $= 5.952\times 10^{32}$ eV, so $\alpha = 5.95$, nearest integer $6$.

pitfalls: Using atomic masses inconsistently (here all given masses are nuclear masses for this accounting).
Forgetting the proton mass on the reactant side.
solution.final_check: $\Delta m = 0.0183$ u per reaction $\times 3.49\times 10^{25}$ reactions gives $5.95\times 10^{32}$ eV — $\alpha = 6$.

subject: physics
stem: A three coulomb charge moves from the point (0, $-2$, $-5$) to the point (5, 1, 2) in an electric field expressed as $\vec{E} = 2x\hat{i} + 3y^2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ N/C. The work done in moving the charge is ______ J.

concepts: Work done by an electric field

steps.text: The field $\vec{E} = 2x\hat{i} + 3y^2\hat{j} + 4\hat{k}$ is conservative (its curl is zero), so the work depends only on the endpoints.
Sum $= 25 + 9 + 28 = 62$ V; $W = 3\times 62 = 186$ J (work done by the field).

pitfalls: Sign confusion: the work done by an external agent moving the charge quasi-statically would be $-186$ J.
Arithmetic slips in the $y^3$ evaluation at the negative limit.
solution.final_check: Potential drop along the path is $62$ V and $q = 3$ C, so $W = 186$ J — dimensionally and numerically consistent.

subject: physics
stem: A certain gas is isothermally compressed to $(\dfrac{1}{3})^{rd}$ of its initial volume ($V_0 = 3$ litre) by applying required pressure. If the bulk modulus of the gas is $3 \times 10^5$ N/m$^2$, the magnitude of work done on the gas is ______ J.

steps.text: For an isothermal change of an ideal gas, the bulk modulus equals the pressure: $B_T = P$. Hence the initial pressure is $P_0 = 3\times 10^5$ Pa.
With $P = P_0V_0/V$ during the isothermal compression, the work done on the gas is $W = \int_{V_0/3}^{V_0}\dfrac{P_0V_0}{V}\,dV = P_0V_0\ln 3$.
$W = 900\times \ln 3 = 900\times 1.0986 = 988.75$ J $\approx 989$ J (nearest integer, as Section B expects an integer).

pitfalls: Using the adiabatic bulk modulus $\gamma P$ instead of the isothermal $P$.
Getting the sign/direction wrong: work done ON the gas is positive in compression.
solution.final_check: $P_0V_0\ln 3 = 988.75$ J is positive and of order $P_0V_0$, as expected for compression to one-third volume — $989$ J.
solution.dispute_note: Our answer is 989 J: for the isothermal expansion, $W = P_0V_0\ln 3 \approx 989\ \mathrm{J}$. The official key says 600, which comes from misapplying the constant-pressure formula. Two independent blind solutions agree on 989.

verification.note: DISPUTE: Two independent blind solves give 989 J (isothermal W=P0V0 ln3); key says 600 (misapplies constant-pressure formula). Published with solver answer.
